vignette: Elias sits on the edge of his leather chair, his knuckles white where they grip his knees. At seventy-five, his hands bear the map of his craft: calloused fingertips, a faint silver scar across the left thumb, and dried clay packed into the whorls of his skin. He describes the day the scaffolding gives way. Three years ago this past October, he stands on a platform, working on a commission-a large bronze figure for a municipal plaza downtown. The metal clamps corrode faster than expected. One moment he smooths the armature; the next, the floor tilts, and he falls forty feet through a construction net that tears like paper. He remembers the sound of his own ribs cracking, the shock of cold pavement, and then the silence. He does not remember the ambulance. In the months that follow, the studio feels like a trap. The sight of hanging chains or swaying pulleys makes his breath catch in tight, shallow pulls. He stops sleeping past two a.m. When he drifts off, his body jolts awake as the mattress dips, mimicking the sudden loss of ground. He remembers when Nadia brings him mint tea. She whispers, "You are home, Elias." After the hospital stay, after the surgeries, after the funeral, her absence becomes a second gravity. He moves her photographs to the top shelf. He does not look at them. When the doorbell rings, his heart hammers against his sternum, and he stands by the window, peeling back the curtain just an inch, assessing who stands on the porch and whether they carry news of loss. His sculptures move with him, heavy and intentional, until they stop. Now he leaves the kiln cold for weeks. When he finally walks into the workspace, the smell of wet clay and mineral oil triggers a wave of nausea that forces him to sit on his stool and count backward from ten. He describes the sensation as a static hum behind his eyes, a tightening in his jaw that he refuses to release, even when his dentist warns him his molars crack from the pressure. He flinches at sudden noises-the drop of a chisel, a car backfiring down the street, the sudden crackle of the radio. Friends who visit note how he scans the room, his eyes tracking exits, his shoulders hunched near his ears. He says that his body still expects the impact. "It does not know I am safe," he replies, his voice flat. "It only knows what it was trained to remember." Over the weeks of their meetings, the studio becomes a quiet theater of his days. He sorts through his tools, aligning the loop knives and rib tools in perfect rows. He speaks in low, measured tones, but the words fracture. He describes a recurring dream where he falls, not through air, but through wet clay, heavy and suffocating, until he wakes gasping, his sheets twisted around his legs like rebar. He stops answering calls from his former patrons. He drives only on familiar routes, keeping his hands at ten and two, his jaw tight. He tends to a small olive tree on his balcony, watering it at the same hour every evening, as if routine can anchor him to the ground. The afternoon light slants through his studio windows, catching the dust motes above his worktable. Elias reaches out and presses his palm against a half-finished piece of marble, feeling its cool, unyielding weight. He does not carve. He simply rests his hand there, listening to the quiet hum of the refrigerator in the next room, the distant murmur of traffic, the steady rhythm of his own breathing. He says that some days, the ground still feels like it is slipping. Other days, it holds. He watches his own reflection in the darkened glass, waits, and continues.
